lesson.menu_desc: Saying which part of the business you look after, when a board asks -- 35 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 1 -- The Person at the Table
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Marcos Aurélio Miranda de Moura | Lesson 1 -- The Person at the Table
lesson.grammar_point: present simple with I, you and we

listenings.text: Good morning, everyone. For the people I have not met, my name is Diane Whitaker and I am the marketing director for the region. I look after five areas. I look after pricing, I look after brand and communication, and I also work with trade marketing, market intelligence and business strategy. My team is small. There are nine of us, and six of them work on the brand side. I report to the group commercial vice president, and I sit on this board every quarter. In a normal week I spend about half my time with the sales teams and the other half with the agencies. Today I bring one item to this meeting, and it is the price list for next year. I know it is the item nobody enjoys, so I keep it short.

People ask me what a good introduction sounds like in a senior meeting, and my answer disappoints them, because it is very short. You say your name. You say what you are responsible for, in one line. You say who you report to, if the room does not already know. And then you stop. That is the whole thing. The mistake I hear every week is the person who explains the entire history of the department before anybody asks for it. Nobody in that room is listening to the history. They are listening for one thing: what does this person decide? A director who says I look after pricing and trade marketing tells me more in six words than a director who talks for two minutes. And one more thing, because it matters for the people who work in a second language. Nobody in a board meeting cares about your grammar. They care whether they understand what you own.

The lubricants business is one of those markets that most people never think about, and it is far bigger than they imagine. Every engine in the country runs on it, from a motorcycle in a small town to a mining truck. The companies that make it do not sell to the driver. They sell to distributors, to workshops and to industry, and that is why you almost never see their advertising. Marketing in this sector is a strange job. The product does not change very often, the price moves with the price of oil, and the customer is usually another company. So the marketing director spends most of the week on two questions. What do we charge, and what does the workshop on the corner say about us when a customer asks? In this market the brand lives in the workshop, and not on television.
